summary: The note describes the nebular hypothesis, the most widely accepted cosmogony model for how the Solar System (and other planetary systems) formed from nebulous material. It was proposed by Immanuel Kant in 1755 and later refined into the solar nebular disk model, largely developed by Victor Safronov and George Wetherill. The note explains which features the model accounts for and notes that most of the original elements have since been superseded.
one_line: Overview of the nebular hypothesis, the leading model of Solar System formation from nebulous material, from Kant's 1755 proposal to the modern solar nebular disk model.
key_facts: The nebular hypothesis is the most widely accepted model in the field of cosmogony for explaining the formation and evolution of the Solar System.
Immanuel Kant developed the theory and published it in Allgemeine Naturgeschichte und Theorie des Himmels in 1755.
The widely accepted modern variant of the nebular hypothesis is the solar nebular disk model (SNDM), also called the solar nebular model.
The solar nebular disk model explains the nearly circular and coplanar orbits of the planets.
The solar nebular disk model explains why the planets orbit in the same direction as the Sun's rotation.
Some elements of the original nebular hypothesis are echoed in modern theories of planetary formation, but most elements have been superseded.
Originally applied to the Solar System, the process of planetary system formation is now thought to be at work throughout the Universe.
The birth of the modern theory of planetary formation can be traced to the Soviet astronomer Victor Safronov.
Victor Safronov's 1969 book Evolution of the protoplanetary cloud and formation of the Earth and the planets was translated into English in 1972.
Safronov's 1969 book formulated almost all major problems of the planetary formation process and solved some of them.
George Wetherill further developed Safronov's ideas and discovered runaway accretion.
As of 1 December 2017, astronomers had discovered 3,710 extrasolar planets in the galaxy.
